newsitem.title: USA: U.N. says Iraq aid plan talks running smoothly.
newsitem.headline: U.N. says Iraq aid plan talks running smoothly.

text.p: U.N. humanitarian aid officials said negotiations to finalize an aid distribution plan necessary for resuming Iraqi "oil-for-food" oil sales are running smoothly and should be finalized by week's end.
A senior U.N. official at New York headquarters said talks between Baghdad and the U.N. are continuing in Iraq, and that all indications point to a successful conclusion.
"They should be done by the end of the week, and be able to send (the aid plan) to New York for the Secretary-General to approve, presumably next week," said the official.
Secretary-General Kofi Annan was expected to receive technical advice on the plan, then approve the document.

"It should go through smoothly. We are trying to make it (the aid plan) better than the last time, improve commodities and proper trucking and proper documentation. It is smooth sailing," said the U.N. official.
Renewed oil sales were expected to start around two weeks after the distribution plan approval, in late July or early August, the official said.
"The oil sales should be another two weeks after (Annan's approval)," said the official.

Staffan de Mistura, the U.N. coordinator for Iraq, has returned to Baghdad after visiting local leaders in the northern, Kurdish regions of the country for their input into the new distribution plan, the U.N. source said.
"He is already back from the north," said U.N. official, noting de Mistura was now working with Iraqi officials in Baghdad.

Iraq has been allowed to sell oil under the second round of the oil accord since June 8, but Baghdad wanted an aid distribution plan in place before starting the oil sales process. Once the distribution plan is settled, Iraq must submit a new pricing formula for oil contracts.

At issue is the so-called "oil-for-food" accord, which acts as a humanitarian exception to broad sanctions slapped on Iraq after its troops invaded Kuwait in 1990. For a 180-day period, Iraq is allowed to sell $2 billion worth of crude oil, with most receipts parlayed into food and medicine purchases for civilians suffering under the sanctions regime.
